items.stem: Which of these numbers is irrational?
items.markingKey: √7 cannot be written as a fraction a/b; √9 = 3, 0.25 = 1/4 and 3/8 are rational.

items.stem: Explain why √16 is rational but √15 is irrational.
items.answer: √16 = 4 = 4/1, which is a fraction of integers; 15 is not a perfect square, so √15 is a non-terminating, non-recurring decimal and cannot be written as a/b.
items.markingKey: B1 √16 = 4 = 4/1 rational; B1 15 not a perfect square so √15 cannot be written as a/b [2]

items.stem: Explain why every integer is a rational number.
items.answer: Any integer n can be written as the fraction n/1, which is a ratio of two integers.
items.markingKey: B1 n = n/1; B1 definition of rational as a/b with integers [2]

items.stem: From the list 16, 33, 27, −7, 23, write down (a) any prime numbers (b) any cube numbers.
From the list 3/7, √5, 3, 25, 33, −12, 125, write down (a) any square numbers (b) any prime numbers (c) any negative integers.
Here is a list of numbers: 30, 100, 53, 343, √8. (a) Find the reciprocal of 1/3 and show that the product of a number and its reciprocal is 1. (b) Explain why 100 is rational and √8 is not.
items.answer: (a) 3; 1/3 × 3 = 1 (b) 100 = 100/1 is a ratio of integers; √8 is a non-recurring, non-terminating decimal that cannot be written as a/b.
items.markingKey: (a) B1 3; B1 shows product = 1 [2] (b) B1 integer as fraction; B1 irrational cannot be a/b [2]

items.stem: Which of these is the reciprocal of 5?
items.markingKey: The reciprocal of n is 1/n, so 5 × 1/5 = 1.

items.stem: Explain why 0 has no reciprocal.
items.answer: The reciprocal of n is 1/n, and division by 0 is undefined; no number multiplied by 0 gives 1.
items.markingKey: B1 1/0 undefined; B1 no number × 0 = 1 [2]

items.stem: Explain why the product of two prime numbers can never be prime.
items.answer: If p and q are prime then pq has factors 1, p, q and pq, so it has more than two factors.
items.markingKey: B1 lists factors p and q; B1 more than two factors so not prime [2]

items.stem: Chloe says "all prime numbers are odd and all odd numbers are prime". Give a counter-example to each part of the statement.
items.answer: 2 is prime but even; 27 is odd but not prime.
items.markingKey: B1 2 is an even prime; B1 an odd composite number with its factor [2]

items.stem: Here is a list of numbers: 71, 36, √30, 125, 144. (a) From the list, write down the prime number. (b) Write 36 as a product of its prime factors. (c) Explain why 144 is rational and √30 is not.
items.answer: (a) 71 (b) 2² × 3² (c) 144 = 144/1 is a ratio of integers; √30 is a non-recurring, non-terminating decimal that cannot be written as a/b.

items.stem: What is the highest common factor of 12 and 18?
items.markingKey: Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12; factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. Highest common = 6.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the HCF and the LCM of two numbers.
items.answer: The HCF is the largest number that divides into both; the LCM is the smallest number that both divide into.
items.markingKey: B1 HCF largest common factor; B1 LCM smallest common multiple [2]

items.stem: Explain how prime factorisations of two numbers can be used to find their LCM.
items.answer: Take every prime that appears in either number, each to the highest power that appears, and multiply them.
items.markingKey: B1 all primes from either; B1 highest power of each [2]

items.stem: Write 28 and 42 as products of prime factors. Hence find (a) the HCF and (b) the LCM of 28 and 42.
items.markingKey: B1 2² × 7; B1 2 × 3 × 7; (a) B1 14 (lowest powers of common primes) (b) B1 84 (highest powers of all primes) [4]

items.markingKey: B1 2³ × 3²; B1 2 × 3² × 5; (a) B1 18 (lowest powers of common primes) (b) B1 360 (highest powers of all primes) [4]

items.stem: A = 2 × 3² × 5 and B = 2 × 3 × 5². (a) Find the lowest common multiple of A and B, giving your answer as a product of prime factors. (b) Find the smallest whole number n such that A × n is a square number.
items.markingKey: (a) M1 highest power of every prime; A1 2 × 3² × 5² [2] (b) M1 identifies odd indices in 2 × 3² × 5; A1 10 [2]

items.stem: What is the lowest common multiple of 4 and 6?
items.markingKey: Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12…; multiples of 6: 6, 12… LCM = 12.

items.stem: Explain why, for any two numbers, HCF × LCM equals the product of the two numbers.
items.answer: Each prime power appears once at its lower index (in the HCF) and once at its higher index (in the LCM), which together give all prime factors of both numbers.
items.markingKey: B1 lower powers in HCF, higher in LCM; B1 together give all factors of the product [2]

items.stem: Two lighthouses flash every 8 seconds and every 12 seconds. Explain whether you would use the HCF or the LCM to find when they next flash together.
items.answer: The LCM, because you need the first time that is a multiple of both 8 and 12 (24 seconds).
items.markingKey: B1 LCM; B1 reason: common multiple of both times (24 s) [2]

items.stem: Mei says that the LCM of 120 and 252 is 120 × 252 = 30240. Explain why this is not correct and find the LCM.
items.answer: 30240 is a common multiple but not the lowest because 120 and 252 share the factor 12. LCM = 30240 ÷ 12 = 2520.
items.markingKey: B1 common factor 12 means a smaller common multiple exists; B1 LCM = 2520 [2]

items.answer: (a) 09:00 (b) No: 480 is a common multiple, but the lowest is 120 minutes, so they coincide every 120 minutes.
items.markingKey: (a) M1 LCM of 6, 8, 10 = 120; A1 09:00 [2] (b) B1 not the lowest; B1 120 [2]

items.stem: What is the value of 2⁵?
Explain why −3² and (−3)² give different answers.
items.answer: In −3² only 3 is squared, giving −9; in (−3)² the whole negative number is squared, giving 9.
items.markingKey: B1 −3² = −9 with reason; B1 (−3)² = 9 [2]

items.stem: Explain why a calculator needs brackets to work out (12 + 8) ÷ 5 correctly.
items.answer: Without brackets the calculator divides first (12 + 8 ÷ 5 = 13.6); brackets force the addition first, giving 20 ÷ 5 = 4.
items.markingKey: B1 division before addition otherwise; B1 correct values 13.6 vs 4 [2]

items.stem: Explain why the square root of a positive number has two values but its cube root has only one real value.
items.answer: Both n × n and (−n) × (−n) give n², so there are two square roots; (−n)³ is negative, so only one real number cubes to a given positive number.
items.markingKey: B1 positive and negative squares equal; B1 negative cube is negative [2]
